Walter Gilbert was awarded the 1980 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, sharing it with Frederick Sanger and Paul Berg, for his pioneering contributions to the determination of base sequences in nucleic acids, commonly known as DNA sequencing.
Paul Nurse was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001 for his discoveries of key regulators of the cell cycle, not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Craig Venter earned both his Bachelor of Science in Biochemistry and his Ph.D. in Physiology and Pharmacology from the University of California, San Diego.

Joseph L. Goldstein received his undergraduate degree from Washington and Lee University and his medical degree from the University of Texas Southwestern Medical School, not the University of California, San Diego.

Richard Owen was a prominent English comparative anatomist and paleontologist, famously known for coining the term 'Dinosauria'. He also served as the superintendent of the natural history departments of the British Museum and was the driving force behind the creation of the Natural History Museum in London.

Alfred Russel Wallace was an independent naturalist, explorer, and writer who primarily made a living by collecting biological specimens and publishing his research. He notoriously struggled to secure formal institutional employment and never worked professionally as a paleontologist, an anatomist, or a museum director.
Victor Frederick Weisskopf was an Austrian-born American theoretical physicist who served as the Director General of CERN from 1961 to 1965.

Robert Oppenheimer never served as the Director General of CERN. He is best known for his role as the director of the Los Alamos Laboratory during the Manhattan Project and later as the director of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.
Carl Sagan earned his undergraduate and graduate degrees from the University of Chicago and won the 1978 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for his book The Dragons of Eden.
Stephen Hawking attended Oxford and Cambridge, not the University of Chicago, and he did not win the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction.
Günter Blobel was awarded the Massry Prize in 1999 for his pioneering research on the mechanisms of protein targeting and translocation.

Joseph L. Goldstein is widely recognized for winning the 1985 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine alongside Michael S. Brown for their discoveries regarding cholesterol metabolism. However, he has not been awarded either the Massry Prize or the Otto Warburg Medal.

Henry Taube received numerous prestigious honors for his work in chemistry, most notably the 1983 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and the Priestley Medal, but he was never awarded the Davy Medal by the Royal Society.

Charles Wyville Thomson was appointed as the Regius Professor of Natural History at the University of Edinburgh in 1870.

William Lawrence Bragg was awarded both the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1915 for his work in X-ray crystallography and the Military Cross for his service developing sound ranging techniques during World War I.

Oliver Smithies was co-awarded the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, along with Mario Capecchi and Martin Evans, for their discoveries of principles for introducing specific gene modifications in mice by the use of embryonic stem cells.
Joan Steitz is a highly distinguished biochemist known for her groundbreaking work on RNA splicing and snRNPs, but she has never been awarded a Nobel Prize.
Maurice Vincent Wilkes both earned his degrees from the University of Cambridge and was the lead designer of the Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator (EDSAC).

Robert E. Kahn earned his degrees from the City College of New York and Princeton University, not the University of Cambridge. James D. Watson was awarded the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, along with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, for their discoveries concerning the molecular structure of nucleic acids.

Frank Albert Cotton was a highly influential inorganic chemist known for his work on metal-metal bonds, but he never received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Theodore von Karman did not attend ETH Zurich. He received his undergraduate degree from the Royal Joseph Technical University in Budapest and earned his doctorate at the University of Gottingen in Germany.
Bert Vogelstein was one of the inaugural recipients of the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences in 2013, recognized for his groundbreaking research on the genetic basis of cancer.

Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac was a renowned French chemist and physicist, famous for his pioneering work on gas laws, the co-discovery of the element boron, and identifying the chemical composition of water.
François Arago was primarily a physicist, mathematician, astronomer, and politician, renowned for his contributions to optics and electromagnetism, rather than chemistry.

Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1995, alongside Eric Wieschaus and Edward B. Lewis, for their discoveries concerning the genetic control of early embryonic development.
Uğur Şahin has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The 2023 Nobel Prize for the development of mRNA vaccine technology was awarded to Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.

Isabella Karle was a highly distinguished American chemist who specialized in X-ray crystallography. She is widely known for her experimental work in developing practical applications for the direct methods used to determine the three-dimensional molecular structure of crystals.

Allen J. Bard specialized in electrochemistry, not crystallography. He is widely considered the 'father of modern electrochemistry' and is famous for his work on the scanning electrochemical microscope.
